messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 63
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Publisher
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 79

He is a 63-year-old man of Oceanian background who has spent most of his adult life in publishing, a profession that has shaped not only his workday but his sense of identity. He is married, and until the event that altered the course of his life, he describes himself as steady, methodical, and able to keep the moving parts of work and family in balance. That changed after the man-made disaster that struck the community he lived and worked in, an event he remembers not as a single moment but as a chain of sounds, images, and frantic decisions that still arrive in his mind without warning.

At the time, he is at his publishing office, reviewing final proofs and answering routine calls when the first signs of trouble begin. At first there is confusion—an unusual noise, people speaking too loudly in the corridor, then the unmistakable sense that something has gone badly wrong. As the situation unfolds, the ordinary structure of the day collapses. He recalls the smell, the shouting, and the sudden rush of people trying to leave, and he remembers realizing, with a cold clarity, that the systems he relied on could fail all at once. He moves through the chaos on instinct, trying to account for staff, get information, and make contact with his wife, but the memory he returns to most is not heroic action; it is helplessness. He speaks of being trapped in a state of urgent attention, unable to think beyond the next minute, while the world around him becomes unrecognizable.

In the weeks that follow, he tells himself he must stay useful. As a publisher, he is accustomed to deadlines, revisions, and contingency plans, and he tries to bring that same order to the aftermath. He returns to work too soon, insisting on checking manuscripts and responding to emails, but he notices that the pages blur when he looks at them. Words that once felt like his element begin to feel foreign and slippery. He rereads the same paragraph over and over, losing the thread. His concentration breaks whenever a door slams in the hallway or a truck backfires outside. The sharp, unexpected noises make his body jolt before his mind can catch up. He begins sitting with his back to the wall, scanning entrances without meaning to, and he keeps one eye on the windows even during ordinary meetings.

At home, he is no longer fully present. His wife notices that he startles easily and that he seems to be listening for danger even in quiet rooms. He sleeps poorly and wakes exhausted, often before dawn, with his heart racing and his mind already searching for what might be wrong. Some nights he sees the event again as he is drifting off: the confusion, the crowding, the impossible sense that something terrible is spreading faster than anyone can control. Other times it returns in fragments during the day, triggered by the smell of smoke, the sound of sirens, or news footage that he cannot seem to stop watching even when he knows it will unsettle him. He avoids certain routes in town, certain conversations, and, for a long time, the office floor where the disaster felt closest. He notices himself taking longer and longer to answer questions because he is quietly measuring whether the answer will lead back to the event.

He is not the same with his colleagues, either. Where he was once patient and even tempered, he now finds himself irritable, cutting conversations short or withdrawing when people expect him to be articulate. He feels guilty for this distance and ashamed of how easily he becomes tense. There are moments when he is flooded with anger at those responsible for the disaster, and moments when that anger turns inward into self-reproach for not having done more. He says the hardest part is the way the event has altered his sense of safety and trust. He still performs the outward role of a publisher, but the work no longer offers the same refuge. Decisions that were once routine now feel weighted with risk, as if one mistake might allow catastrophe back in.

Over time, he continues to function, but in a narrowed way. He keeps to predictable routines, checks locks more than once, and avoids being caught in crowds. He and his wife remain close, though she has learned that he may go quiet in the middle of a conversation when a memory or sensation overtakes him. In recent sessions, he describes living with a persistent sense that part of him is still in the aftermath, waiting for the next disruption. He speaks with the careful precision of a man used to words, yet there is grief in the way he describes how much effort it now takes to get through an ordinary day.
